title: Part over Whole
context: Grade 5, the pages on one number as a per cent of another. An adult sees a formula. What the pages are doing is naming a part against its whole: the part over the whole, made into hundredths. Both amounts are written in the same unit first, a match not won may have been a draw, and the opening question can be tried here, with its answer left to the child.

writeup.why: Write one number as a per cent of another by putting the part over the whole, with the bracketed rule, both amounts in one unit first, and tell the matches not won from the matches counted against a team.
writeup.look: A whole bar labelled 100% over a part bar at the same scale. The fraction card and the Rule button stand beside them, with the Unit fact card, and on the last phase a row of match tiles.
writeup.stage: Three bands across 1600 by 900. The header runs 0 to 80 and is one line only: 'Part over Whole' in ink at the far left, a small dot set clear of the name, the phase title beside the dot on the same line, the host's navigation, and sound and restart as three round controls at the far right. The canvas runs 92 to 746, one rounded card on the paper colour. At its top left, at x 64, y 108 and 330 by 76, sits the running count: the per cent of the whole bar that the part covers. It is never a score. The working area is 1086 by 528 at x 64, y 202. The whole bar lies at x 110, y 240, 900 long and 70 tall, labelled Whole and 100%, and the part bar lies under it at x 110, y 330, drawn to the same scale in deep blue, labelled Part. The fraction card stands at x 110, y 440 with the Times buttons in a row beside it; when both terms grow, the words Both terms light vermilion. The Rule button builds its brackets at x 110, y 560, the times one hundred step vermilion and the % sign in ink after the closing bracket, and the per cent reached is green. The Unit fact card stands at x 700, y 440 and rewrites an amount in violet. For several parts of one whole, each part takes its own band on the whole bar with its per cent written on it. On the fourth phase the match tiles, each 70 by 70, lie in a row at y 250 and are dragged into a Won row at y 400 and a Not won row at y 520, the Not won row rose; a tile turned over shows the word Draw. Down the right of the canvas, in the same rectangle on every phase and never animated in or out, the question sits above the answer slot at x 1186, y 250 (356 by 92) that holds what the child has given, and under it the pad at x 1170, y 368 (388 by 363). The pad is ten number keys with a fraction bar key, a point key, a % key and unit keys. The footer runs 758 to 900: the voice caption at the far left with its speaking dot beside it, measuring its own wrap and dropping a type size rather than spilling, and the phase bar at the right with the question count under it. There is no sidebar and no score box anywhere, and nothing is ever written over the working area. Content colours are the chapter's own, and the tools of this chapter share them. The part the question gives, as shaded cells, a fraction, a decimal or an amount, is deep blue, labelled Given. The per cent, fraction or decimal the working reaches, and what is left after a part is used, is green, labelled Answer or Left. Both terms multiplied or divided by one number, and the times one hundred step before the % sign, are vermilion, labelled Both terms or Times 100. A unit fact that puts two amounts in one unit is violet, labelled Unit fact. The part used, taken away or not won is rose, labelled Used or Not won. The step, cell or number being worked on now is amber. A zero holding a place open inside a decimal is grey, labelled Place holder, and nothing else on the stage is ever grey. An unshaded cell of a whole stays warm white inside its near-black outline, the % sign is near-black ink, and anything dimmed fades to half strength rather than turning grey. Chrome never borrows one of them, and each reading survives with the colour taken away, because a part is told by its written label before it is told by its colour.
writeup.finish: The bars show the last part against its whole, the bracketed line under them, and the unit fact that was used.

writeup.delight: On the third phase, the moment the Unit fact card is dropped, the whole bar's label rewrites itself in violet, and the part bar shrinks to its true length and settles against the whole with a soft click.
writeup.opening: Every mount comes up already furnished for its phase with nothing yet tapped. On the first phase the whole bar holds beads of several colours, with the fraction card blank. On the second the question card asks what per cent one number is of another, with the Rule button lit. On the third the whole bar and the part bar carry amounts in two units, the part bar too long to lie against the whole. On the fourth a row of match tiles waits, some marked won and some turned to show a draw. One thing moves, once: the first control the phase needs gives one slow pulse while the voice speaks its opening line.
writeup.freePlay: A part and a whole of the child's own, in one unit or two, and any row of match tiles. Nothing to get right, no target and no timer. The child is left with the same stage and every control unlocked.
writeup.practice: Eight items over the four phases, easy first, on parts of a whole, the bracketed rule, amounts in two units, and matches not won.

source_tool.description: Two bars lie across the working area, one above the other, drawn to one scale: the whole bar, labelled Whole and 100%, and the part bar under it in deep blue, labelled Part. A Part over whole button writes the part over the whole as a fraction on a card, and the Times buttons of the chapter, times two, four, five, ten, twenty, twenty-five and fifty, grow both terms until the denominator is 100, lighting the words Both terms vermilion. A Rule button builds the formula in brackets, the first number over the second times 100, and writes the % sign after the closing bracket; the per cent reached is green. A Unit fact card, chosen from a short list, rewrites an amount in violet, such as 1 kg = 1000 g or 1 litre = 1000 mL, and the bars cannot be laid against each other until both amounts are in one unit. For several parts of one whole, each part takes its own colour band on the whole bar, with its per cent written on it. On the last phase a row of match tiles is sorted by drag into Won and Not won, and a tile can be turned to show a draw. A number pad types any number, amount or per cent. The running count at the top left of the canvas is the per cent of the whole bar that the part covers.
source_tool.art_direction: Beads, bars and match tiles / Picture book

audio.note: Web Audio oscillators, no files. The same three cues in every tool of every Class 5 chapter, so the grade sounds like one grade.

wrong.note: A soft low double-bloop. A nudge, never a buzzer.

modes.freePlay: Out of scope here. It is not reached from inside a phase mount, because a phase mount ends idle and has no finish card to reach it from. writeup.freePlay stays as the record of what that activity is, for whoever builds it as its own thing.

style.text: Least text. One header line, short labels, nothing else. The voice carries the teaching and the caption carries the voice.

stage.note: Every coordinate is authored in 1600x900, so a smartboard and a phone in landscape get one composition. Nothing scrolls. The three bands below are the settled layout, taken from Two Hundred Trail in Class 3 chapter 3 once it was finished; a tool that has to depart from one of them says in its own writeup.stage which band it changed and why.

bands.canvas: 92 to 746. One rounded panel holding everything the child works on.
bands.footer: 758 to 900. The voice at the far left, the phase bar at the right.
bands.header: 0 to 80. One line, and only one.

zones.bar: the phase bar at the right of the footer, the question count under it
zones.pad: under the slot, and furniture on every phase: twelve keys three across where a number is asked for, a word pad where a name or a rule is
zones.name: the tool name at the far left of the header, a measured dot set clear of it
zones.runs: the running count, on the canvas at its top left, never up in the chrome. It counts the thing the tool is actually building; where a tool has nothing to count that corner carries the record being kept instead, and that tool's own stage says so
zones.slot: the question and the child's answer, fixed down the right of the canvas
zones.work: the working area, one thousand and eighty-six by five hundred and twenty-eight
zones.title: the phase title beside that dot, on the same single header line
zones.voice: the caption at the far left of the footer, its speaking dot beside it
zones.chrome: again, sound and restart, as round controls at the far right of the header

stage.furniture: The working area is furnished from the first frame. What waits for the child is the count, not the picture: the panels, the slot and the pad are all up and empty before anything is asked.
stage.noSidebar: There is no sidebar. The canvas takes every unit the chrome can spare, because the working area is the tool.
stage.noScoreBox: There is no score box anywhere on the stage. The score leaves on the finished event and it is the host that decides whether to show it, so a child working is never watching a number that judges them.

style.motion: Animate only what carries meaning. Anything that is not changing does not move. Every reward is the maths itself moving, never confetti. Honour prefers-reduced-motion.
drawing: Hand-built inline SVG. No assets and no network, so a school cart works offline.
Chunky rounded forms and large touch targets. A finger is the pointer, not a mouse.

Drawn things, not abstract boxes: hundred grids of ten rows and ten columns, strips cut into equal cells, fraction bars with their denominator of one hundred built beside them, measuring jugs, tapes and scales with their units written on them.

Every whole is drawn the same size as every other whole it is compared with, and its parts are exactly equal: a strip of ten has ten cells of one width, and a hundred grid is always a full ten by ten.
A whole is always labelled 100%, so the child sees what one hundred per cent means before any part is named.
Where shaded cells are counted, exactly the stated number is shaded, and they stay countable at a glance: full columns of ten first, then single cells.
A product that becomes a per cent is always written with its brackets, and the % sign comes last. A decimal reaches a per cent through its hundredths, never by moving anything.
Nothing is animated except the one thing being explained: cells filling a grid, both terms of a fraction growing together, a unit fact rewriting an amount, or a used part lifting away.
style.palette_rule: A chrome colour never fills a cell or a number the child is reading, and a content colour is never used for chrome. This chapter colours the roles a per cent plays in a piece of working: the part the question gives, as shaded cells, a fraction, a decimal or an amount, is deep blue, and the per cent, fraction or decimal the working reaches, with what is left after a part is used, is green; those two are the same two in every tool and every picture of this chapter. Both terms multiplied or divided by one number, and the times one hundred step before the % sign, are vermilion. A unit fact that puts two amounts in one unit is violet. The part used, taken away or not won is rose. The step, cell or number being worked on now is amber. A zero holding a place open inside a decimal is grey. An unshaded cell of a whole stays warm white inside its outline, and the % sign itself is near-black ink. Each role is named in writing first, with the words Given, Answer, Both terms, Unit fact, Used, Not won, Left and Place holder, so the stage still reads with the colour taken away.

rules: Every spoken line is also printed in the caption line at the far left of the footer, so a muted tablet and a child who cannot hear lose nothing.
The caption stays in the footer. Nothing is ever written over the working area.

Numbers are written as words in every line and never as digits, so the voice says four steps and not 4 steps. Handed a digit, a synthesiser reads it in whatever register it likes and the chapter loses the words it is teaching.
The voice never gives the answer. It asks the same question a different way.
It speaks on opening, once when a phase begins, on a miss, and at the finish. It is silent otherwise; a tool that chatters gets muted, and then the first rule is all that is left.
props.muted is honoured at the source, and turning sound off cancels any line already speaking.
voice.where: The caption line sits at the far left of the footer with a small dot beside it that glows while the voice is talking. An again control repeats the last line.
voice.figure: None. The voice speaks with nothing on the stage.
voice.onMiss: Name the whole again, then put the part over it.
voice.onNext: A new part and whole. Which one is the whole?
voice.opening: A whole, and a part to lay against it.
voice.onFinish: Every part found its per cent against its own whole.
voice.onFreePlay: Free play. Lay any part against any whole.
voice.figure_rule: A figure appears only where the printed chapter puts one and it has work to do. Everywhere else the voice speaks from the caption line with nothing on the stage: a mascot with no job is one more thing competing with the quantities the child is looking at.
voice.voicePreference: an English voice, female where one is offered

placement.where: After the class has counted some group of their own, such as who walked to school, and written it over the number asked. The tool is what lays the part against the whole to scale and rewrites a unit before the two are compared, which paper can only describe.

answer_key.rule: Name the whole first. Write the part over the whole and make the denominator 100, or use the rule: the first number over the second, times 100, in brackets, then the % sign. The parts of one whole, as per cents, make 100% together. First write both amounts in the same unit, and say the unit fact used, such as 1 kg = 1000 g. A match that was not won may have been a draw, so not won counts as lost only when every match was either won or lost. The question in the opening box is the child's to answer.
answer_key.wrong: The part bar is laid again against the whole bar at the same scale, with the child's per cent drawn as a second part beside it, so the two lengths are seen side by side, and the step where they part is lit amber. Nothing is cleared and nothing is marked.

hostProps.muted: Sound off. Honour it at the source, not by muting an element later. The captions carry on.
hostProps.phase: number, 1-based, which phase to build. The host chooses the activity; the component builds that phase and nothing else and never moves on by itself.
hostProps.device: tablet / web / smartboard. The stage is a fixed 1600x900 that scales; lay nothing out per device.
hostProps.audience: classroom or solo, and ACCEPTED AND NOT ACTED ON. The teach run and the hint ladder run either way. Kept so the contract is one shape across the book, and named here so nobody reads the shape as a promise.
hostProps.learnQuestions: The four worked items, one per phase, supplied by the host.
hostProps.practiceQuestions: The eight practice items, supplied by the host.

phase_mount.run: A phase is a complete activity in itself and it runs once. The teaching and the doing are not two screens and not two modes: the stage is furnished once, the voice talks over it, and the child starts working on the same stage without anything being rebuilt. Whatever the tool as a whole has to say goes into the FIRST phase's teach run, because there is no opening screen to say it on.
phase_mount.idle: NO AUTO-ADVANCE. After firing, the tool goes idle on the settled phase with the child's work still on it, and stops. Where the host supplies onNext it is drawn and it calls the host back; nothing in the component advances a phase.
phase_mount.prop: phase: number, 1-based, matching writeup.phases[].n. Rounded, clamped, and defaulting to 1 when the host sends nothing, so a bare mount is still a working tool rather than a blank screen. Read once: changing which phase a mount shows is a re-mount.
phase_mount.rule: ONE PHASE, ONE MOUNT. The host says which phase to build by passing `phase`, and the component builds that phase and nothing else. It does not know what came before it and it never moves on by itself.
phase_mount.opening: There is no opening panel and no Start button. The host has already chosen the activity, and a cover screen in front of it is a click between a child and the work. writeup.opening is the first frame of every mount rather than a panel of its own.
phase_mount.completion: The terminal event `finished`, with the phase in its detail, fired exactly once and guarded by a one-shot ref that only a restart re-arms, with the chime and the settle OUTSIDE the guard. props.onComplete is called alongside it: the event is the platform's signal and the callback is the host wrapper's, and firing only one of them leaves a child on a tool that never completes.
phase_mount.notInAMount: No finish card and no free play. Both are the host's now, built out of what the events told it. writeup.finish and writeup.freePlay stay as the record of what they are.

shared_state.note: What getState() returns. These names are a contract: the host reads them to persist and resume a child mid-activity, so renaming one breaks resume. `mode` is gone from this list because there is no mode. `phase` is the phase the host mounted, so a resume restores the work inside a phase and the host restores which phase.

agent_control.reason: Every tool in this chapter is child-operated. There is no agent-driven Concept mode, no postMessage command channel and no narration the tool waits on; the adult, where there is one, talks over the tool rather than through it.

steps: Write the part over the whole: 23/50.
In the same way, the roses are 38% and the lilies 16%, and the three per cents make 100% together.
items.question: A garden bed has 50 plants: 23 marigolds, 19 roses and 8 lilies. What per cent of the plants are marigolds?
items.checkpoint: The parts of one whole, as per cents, make 100% together.
items.misconception: Writing 23/27, the marigolds over the other plants, instead of over all 50.

steps: Put the first number over the second: 26/40.
Multiply by 100 inside the brackets, and write the % sign after them.
items.question: What per cent is 26 of 40?
items.checkpoint: The first number over the second, times 100, in brackets, then the % sign.
items.misconception: Putting the second number over the first, 40/26, which gives more than one whole for a part.

steps: First write both amounts in the same unit.
1 litre = 1000 mL, so 5 litres make 5000 mL.
items.question: What per cent of 5 litres is 1200 mL?
items.checkpoint: First write both amounts in the same unit, and say the unit fact used.
items.misconception: Writing 1200/5, which mixes millilitres with litres and gives far more than one whole.

steps: A match can end in a draw, so not won counts as lost only if every match was either won or lost.
items.question: A team played 25 matches and won 17. What per cent of its matches did it not win?
items.checkpoint: Not won counts as lost only when every match was either won or lost.
items.misconception: Giving 68%, the per cent won, when the question asks for the matches not won.

learn.shape: Worked items, shown solved, mandatory before practice unlocks.
learn.selection: Fixed order, walking the phases from the first to the last.
learn.content_criterion: One per phase, so Learn walks the whole topic and stops.

items.question: A box has 10 beads: 7 red and 3 blue. What per cent of the beads are red?
What per cent of 1 m is 40 cm?
items.final_answer: 40%. 1 m = 100 cm, and 40 cm out of 100 cm is 40%

items.question: A team played 20 matches and won 16. What per cent of its matches did it not win?
items.final_answer: 20%. 4 of the 20 matches were not won, and 4 of 20 is 20%

items.question: A tray has 60 cups: 27 white and 33 green. What per cent of the cups are white?
Use the rule with brackets to find what per cent 27 is of 30.
What per cent of 3 kg is 360 g?
A team played 50 matches and won 31, and every match was either won or lost. What per cent of its matches did it lose?
items.final_answer: 38%. 50 - 31 = 19 matches were not won, and since every match was either won or lost, 19 were lost: 19/50 = 38/100, which is 38%

teaching_notes: Count a group of the class's own before the tool opens, and write the part over the number asked. Name the whole first every time. Write the brackets: the first number over the second, times 100, then the % sign. Put both amounts in the same unit first, and say the unit fact aloud. A match not won may be a draw, so ask which the question wants. The opening question can be tried now, and its answer is the child's own. Use fresh numbers: the exercise's pairs are the child's to work.
generation_prompt: Build a part over whole tool on a fixed 1600x900 SVG stage. A whole bar, labelled Whole and 100%, lies over a part bar in deep blue, both drawn to one scale. A Part over whole button writes the fraction on a card, and Times buttons grow both terms until the denominator is 100, lighting the words Both terms vermilion. A Rule button builds the first number over the second times 100 in brackets and writes the % sign after the closing bracket; the per cent reached is green. A Unit fact card rewrites an amount in violet, such as 1 kg = 1000 g, and the bars cannot be compared until both are in one unit. Several parts of one whole each take a colour band on the whole bar. On the last phase a row of match tiles is dragged into Won and Not won, and a tile can show a draw. A number pad types numbers, amounts and per cents. The running count at the top left of the canvas is the per cent the part covers. Pointer events only, no assets, no network. Build it from the writeup and the tool build spec, not from this paragraph (maths_agent/TOOL_BUILD_SPEC.md). The three bands and every measurement come from writeup.stage and tool_config.style.stage: one header line, one canvas panel holding everything the child works on with the running count at its top left and the question, slot and pad fixed down its right as furniture, and a footer with the voice at the far left and the phase bar at the right. No sidebar, and no score box anywhere. One phase, one mount: build the phase the host passes and nothing else (tool_config.phase_mount). The first frame comes from writeup.opening. Each phase comes from writeup.phases, with its screen, action, reward and spoken line; its tries field is the hint ladder and its wrong list is what the stage does about a wrong answer, redrawn in steps on the working area with nothing marked and nothing reset. The one surprise is writeup.delight. The look and the sounds come from tool_config.style, voice and audio.
